input:
This worked example is concerned with the calculation of the friction pressure drop that occurs when water flows through a horizontal pipe, which is a very common situation in process engineering practice. The water is at a temperature of 293 K and has a density, denoted by $\rho$, of 998 kg m-3. The flow conditions and the pipe dimensions are as follows: the mean velocity of the water, denoted by $v$, is 1.6 m s-1, the pipe diameter, denoted by $D$, is 0.1 m, the pipe length, denoted by $L$, is 84 m and the Darcy friction factor, denoted by $f$, is 0.02. The relationship that connects these quantities to the friction pressure drop is the Darcy-Weisbach relation, which is written in the following form:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

When the numerical values that have been listed above are substituted into this equation in a careful and systematic manner, the friction pressure drop for the pipe is found to be 21.5 kPa. This figure represents the pressure energy that is lost purely as a result of friction between the moving water and the pipe wall over the full length of the run, and because the pipe is horizontal, there is no additional contribution from a change in elevation to be taken into account in this particular calculation. The example also illustrates a more general point about pipe-flow calculations of this kind, namely that the friction loss accumulates steadily along the entire length of the run, so that long pipelines of modest diameter can generate surprisingly large pressure duties even at velocities (in m s-1) that appear, at first sight, to be quite moderate and unremarkable.
target:
Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe, and the friction pressure drop is calculated from the Darcy-Weisbach relation, in which $\Delta P$ denotes the pressure drop (Pa), $f$ denotes the Darcy friction factor, $L$ denotes the pipe length (m), $D$ denotes the pipe diameter (m), $\rho$ denotes the density and $v$ denotes the mean velocity (m s-1):

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3, the mean velocity $v$ is 1.6 m s-1, the diameter $D$ is 0.1 m, the length $L$ is 84 m and the friction factor $f$ is 0.02. Substitution gives a friction pressure drop of 21.5 kPa. Because the pipe is horizontal, no elevation term enters: the result is the whole pressure loss over the run, and it is the figure a pump or a gravity head must supply to hold the stated velocity in this pipe. The velocity carries the largest sensitivity in the result. The pressure drop varies with the square of $v$, so a modest rise in throughput costs disproportionately more pressure, while the friction factor enters only in direct proportion. The calculation takes $f$ as given; in an application the factor would itself be read from the flow regime and the pipe roughness, and an error there passes into $\Delta P$ unchanged in proportion. Length and diameter enter as a ratio, and the ratio is what the designer trades: a larger diameter at the same velocity lowers the loss in direct proportion to the ratio change, before the further benefit of the lower velocity that a larger bore brings at fixed volumetric flow is counted. The worked figure is therefore best read as one point on that trade-off, fixed by the stated geometry, rather than as a property of water flow in general.
